name: Esther Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for making the time, Esther. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is confidential. Is that all right with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I like talking about this, my husband says I don't talk about anything else lately.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Then tell me what a normal working day looks like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior tele-remote operator at an underground copper and zinc mine. That means I drive a loader, the machine that scoops broken ore after a blast, from a chair on the surface, using cameras and a joystick, while the machine is eight hundred metres below me. I run three loaders across a shift and I'm the one who trains the others on the system. The best bit is that I can clear a stope, which is the open space left after blasting, straight after the blast without waiting for the fumes to clear, so nobody's breathing that. What wears me out is the screens, staring at grainy camera feeds for ten hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we got some good tools and the world didn't end, which is about right. I'd say it in the women-in-mining group I run online, and probably at church too, because people there ask me about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I'm already where the technology is, and I'd keep getting better at it. Nothing to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep training operators, and I'd keep building the small consulting side I've started, helping smaller mines set up tele-remote. Daniel and I would keep saving for a bigger house, and probably start a family next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Where does it fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to review my camera footage for near misses, to write training guides, and to plan the loader routes. I teach the machines on weekdays and Sunday school on Sundays, and honestly the kids are harder. It's a tool like any other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything outside work you're building?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The consulting. I've done two jobs for small mines in the region, setting up their tele-remote systems. It's small, but I'd like it to grow into a family business one day.

S0.say: She'd say the world got some good tools and didn't end, which is about right. She'd share that in the women-in-mining group she runs online and at church, where people ask her about it.
S0.think: She thinks it's fine for her, since she already works where the technology is and would keep improving, with nothing to lose.
S0.do: Keeps training operators and grows her small consulting work helping smaller mines set up tele-remote systems. Keeps saving with her husband Daniel for a bigger house and plans to start a family next year.
S0.quote: I teach the machines on weekdays and Sunday school on Sundays, and honestly the kids are harder.
S0.fieldNote: Esther blends early adoption of technology with a strong faith and community life. She already runs a small consulting sideline and dreams of it becoming a family business. She sees AI as just another tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and people should get ahead of it, not wait for the government to fix it. Learn the new systems, help each other. That's what I'd tell the women in my group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a good picture for me. More mines would want tele-remote and automation, and I know how to set it up. I'd probably earn more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine to let me run the automation training full-time, and I'd register the consulting business properly and take on more clients. I'd learn the newest AI tools for fleet scheduling. I'd invest some savings in better equipment for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some of your colleagues may struggle with this. What would you do for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run free evening sessions at the church hall for miners who want to learn the systems. Nobody should lose their job because they were too proud to ask a 27-year-old woman for help. I'd be patient with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the mine to consult full-time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. I'd grow it on the side for a couple of years. When the consulting matched my wage, then I'd go.

S1.say: She'd say change is coming and people should get ahead of it rather than wait for government. She'd tell the women in her group to learn the new systems and help each other.
S1.think: She sees it as good for her because more mines would want tele-remote and automation, which she knows how to set up, and she'd likely earn more.
S1.do: Asks to run automation training full-time, registers her consulting business and takes on more clients. Learns the newest AI fleet-scheduling tools, invests savings in training equipment, and runs free evening sessions at the church hall.
S1.quote: Nobody should lose their job because they were too proud to ask a 27-year-old woman for help.
S1.fieldNote: Esther is ready to gain in this picture and wants to bring others along through community, especially church. Her traditional values show in self-reliance over government help. She'd move to full-time consulting only once it matched her wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when families and communities have to stick together. Government can't do it all, and it shouldn't. Churches, families, neighbours, that's who gets people through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job and my business go together, because an AI could set up tele-remote faster than me. I'd be all right for money for a while, but I'd lose what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to sell as much consulting as I could while it's still wanted, and put the earnings into land and something solid. I'd keep the savings in safe places. And Daniel and I would probably start a family sooner, while we still had good jobs and good health cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for the money, for the purpose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the consulting business survive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year, maybe two, as the last wave of mines catch up. After that, no. AI does the consulting too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned starting a family. Does this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, sooner, not later. If the world turns upside down in two years, I'd rather be holding a baby than waiting for a better time that won't come.

S2.say: She'd say this is when families and communities must stick together, because government can't and shouldn't do it all. Churches, families and neighbours get people through.
S2.think: She thinks her job and her business go together because AI could set up tele-remote faster than her. Money would last, but she'd lose what she's good at.
S2.do: Sells as much consulting as she can in the two years and puts the earnings into land and safe savings. Starts a family sooner with Daniel while they still have good jobs and health cover.
S2.feel: Anxious, not about money but about purpose.
S2.quote: If the world turns upside down in two years, I'd rather be holding a baby than waiting for a better time that won't come.
S2.fieldNote: Esther's worry in this picture is about meaning rather than money. Her traditional values steer her toward community and family, not the state. She'd actually bring forward having a child, reasoning that waiting wouldn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to build something, so build it. Families and towns should be planning now, not waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can grow the consulting into something real before it's done by AI. And use what I earn to set our family up properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd go full-time on the consulting, hire two of the best operators I've trained, and take contracts across the region. I'd learn the AGI tools as they come out, so I'm the one selling them, not competing with them. We'd buy a small property with land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A family business that sets up automation for mines, then for farms and towns. If the robots are coming either way, better they come through people who know the town and go to church with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What role would your church play?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A big one. I'd help the church set up a job board and a training night. People will need somewhere to go that isn't a screen.

S3.say: She'd say five years is time to build something, and families and towns should be planning now rather than waiting.
S3.think: She thinks she can grow the consulting into something real before AI takes it over, and use the earnings to set her family up properly.
S3.do: Goes full-time on consulting in the first year, hires two of the best operators she's trained and takes contracts across the region. Learns new AGI tools as they arrive, buys a small property with land, and helps her church set up a job board and training night.
S3.quote: If the robots are coming either way, better they come through people who know the town and go to church with you.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Esther pictures a family business bringing automation to mines, farms and towns through local, trusted people. She frames technology through community and faith. Her church becomes part of her plan, not just a refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it well. Start families, build businesses, look after your neighbours. Don't sit around waiting for a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I have time for everything. Children, a business, a home, and to help other people get ready too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep my mine job and grow the consulting on the side. Around year three, I'd go full-time and hire people. By year six, I'd want the business running across mines and farms and our house paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I can see the whole road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years puts you at thirty-seven. Who are you then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mother, a business owner, probably still teaching Sunday school. I'd want my kids to see their mother build something, not just watch the news about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a young woman starting in mining today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the machines and learn people. The machines will change, but you'll always need to know how to talk to a crew.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a gift to use well by starting families, building businesses and looking after neighbours rather than waiting for a handout.
S4.think: She thinks ten years gives her time for everything: children, a business, a home, and helping others prepare.
S4.do: Keeps her mine job in year one while growing the consulting on the side, goes full-time and hires around year three, and aims for a business spanning mines and farms and a paid-off house by year six.
S4.feel: Calm, because she can see the whole road.
S4.quote: I'd want my kids to see their mother build something, not just watch the news about it.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Esther's adaptability and her traditional values point the same way. She pictures herself as mother, business owner and Sunday school teacher at 37. Her advice to young women is about both machines and people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build anything before it all moves. What would help is support for small local businesses to buy and run the new machines, and for families to keep their homes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what work is for. My grandmother said work is how you love your neighbour on a weekday. If the robots do the work, we'll have to find another way.

headlineQuote: My grandmother said work is how you love your neighbour on a weekday. If the robots do the work, we'll have to find another way.
portrait: Esther Khan is 27, the senior tele-remote operator at an underground copper and zinc mine, driving loaders from a surface chair and training others on the system. She is married to Daniel, teaches Sunday school, runs an online women-in-mining group and has a small consulting sideline setting up tele-remote systems for smaller mines. She uses AI every day and is calm, even excited, in the milder pictures, anxious about purpose rather than money when AGI comes in two years, and uneasy then calm with five or ten years. Her answer to every AGI picture is family, faith and a family business that brings automation to her region through trusted local people.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there would be no time to build anything before everything moved.
whatWouldHelp: Support for small local businesses to buy and run the new machines, and for families to keep their homes.
